summary: Defines RADIUS support for the Extensible Authentication Protocol. A network access server passes EAP packets to and from the RADIUS server, wrapped in RADIUS messages, so many authentication methods can be used without the access server understanding each. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A building guard can let a call center check IDs of many kinds without learning each ID type. This memo lets a network box pass any kind of login check along to a central server.

questions: how does eap work with radius
subtitle: How a network access server can pass any EAP login method to a RADIUS server without understanding it.

tldr.problem: A network access server (NAS) should not need new code for every authentication method that EAP can carry.
tldr.mechanism: The NAS wraps EAP packets in RADIUS EAP-Message attributes and forwards them to the RADIUS server, protecting every such packet with a Message-Authenticator attribute.
tldr.outcome: Method-specific code lives on the RADIUS server, and the NAS just obeys its Accept or Reject. The memo is Informational and was later updated by RFC 5080.

today: RFC 3579 is an Informational memo that updates RFC 2869, and it was later updated by RFC 5080. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RADIUS is an authentication, authorization and accounting protocol used to control network access. EAP, the Extensible Authentication Protocol, is a framework that supports multiple authentication mechanisms on dedicated links, switched circuits, and wired and wireless links. The memo notes it had been used with PPP and with IEEE 802 bridges.

This document describes two RADIUS attributes that support EAP, EAP-Message and Message-Authenticator. They already had extensive field experience, and the stated purpose is to clarify and resolve interoperability issues. The memo updates RFC 2869.

A NAS that does not offer EAP service MUST NOT implement the EAP attributes, and MUST treat an Access-Accept that requests an unavailable service as an Access-Reject.
sections.eli5: RADIUS is the office that says yes or no to people joining a network. EAP is a menu of ways to prove who you are. This memo explains how the two work together.

sections.title: How RADIUS Carries EAP
sections.content:
The NAS acts as a pass-through. It negotiates EAP with the peer (the user device being authenticated), usually sends an EAP-Request/Identity, and puts the peer's EAP-Response into EAP-Message attributes inside a RADIUS Access-Request. The server replies with an Access-Challenge carrying the next EAP request, and the exchange continues until the server sends an Access-Accept or Access-Reject. EAP is a lock-step protocol: apart from the initial request, a new request is not sent before a valid response arrives.

An Access-Reject MUST result in the NAS denying access. The NAS MUST NOT make up an EAP Success or Failure on a timeout; after enough timeouts it SHOULD end the conversation instead. A NAS may also authenticate local users itself, but once it starts passing a session through to RADIUS it can no longer authenticate that session locally.

So that proxies that do not understand EAP can still route the request, the NAS MUST copy the identity from the EAP-Response/Identity into the User-Name attribute and keep it in every later Access-Request. Alternatively, the NAS MAY open with an Access-Request carrying an EAP-Start, an EAP-Message of length 2 with no data, but this SHOULD NOT be the default where many peers are EAP unaware, since it can cause many conversations that never complete.
sections.eli5: The guard at the door hands you a question from the call center, passes your answer back, and so on. The guard never has to understand the questions. At the end the call center says let them in or keep them out.

sections.title: Errors, Retransmission and Usage Rules
sections.content:
While passing packets through, the NAS MUST check the EAP Code, Identifier and Length fields. Responses that do not match the current Identifier are silently discarded. Because the NAS does not look inside the method data, a bad packet can still be forwarded. For a fatal error the RADIUS server MUST send an Access-Reject carrying an EAP Failure. For a non-fatal one it MAY send an Access-Challenge with an Error-Cause attribute of value 202, "Invalid EAP Packet (Ignored)". Against denial of service, a server is advised to allow only a modest number of invalid EAP packets in a session, with 5 recommended by default.

A server can set the EAP retransmission timer for a single request by putting a Session-Timeout attribute in the Access-Challenge, which helps, for example, when a user must find a token card. For large EAP packets, the NAS may send a Framed-MTU attribute so the server never sends EAP-Message attributes whose concatenated length exceeds it.

Usage guidelines include: each EAP session has its own Identifier space; role reversal is not supported, so a server MUST answer an Access-Request carrying an EAP-Request with an Access-Reject; and the NAS MUST decide access solely from the RADIUS packet type (Accept or Reject), never from the encapsulated EAP packet. A server SHOULD NOT send contradictory combinations, such as Access-Accept with an EAP Failure. Text for the user belongs in an EAP Notification, and a NAS SHOULD silently discard Reply-Message attributes.
sections.eli5: The guard checks that each note is numbered correctly and has not been torn. The guard only listens to the call center's yes or no, not to whatever is written on the note, so mixed-up messages do not confuse who gets in.

sections.title: The EAP-Message and Message-Authenticator Attributes
sections.content:
EAP-Message is attribute type 79 with a length of at least 3. Its string holds an EAP packet. If a packet is longer than 253 octets, it is split across several consecutive EAP-Message attributes, in order, and the values are concatenated. Multiple EAP packets MUST NOT be encoded in a single RADIUS packet.

Message-Authenticator is attribute type 80 with a length of 18. It is an HMAC-MD5 hash of the packet using the shared secret as the key, computed with the attribute's own 16 octets treated as zero. Any packet that contains an EAP-Message MUST also contain a Message-Authenticator. A receiver that supports EAP-Message MUST check the value and silently discard the packet if it does not match. This protects against attackers changing items such as EAP Success or Failure.

An Access-Request carrying a password-type attribute or EAP-Message MUST NOT contain more than one of the four types: User-Password, CHAP-Password, ARAP-Password or EAP-Message.
sections.eli5: Each wrapped note gets a tamper-proof seal made with a secret that only the guard and the call center know. A note with a missing or wrong seal is thrown away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Both the RADIUS and the EAP parts of the conversation are targets. The memo lists threats such as snooping, modifying or injecting packets, dictionary and known plaintext attacks on the shared secret, replay, disrupting EAP negotiation, forged NAS identification, rogue NAS impersonation and man-in-the-middle attacks. Meeting them needs per-packet confidentiality, data origin authentication, integrity and replay protection, plus two-way authentication between client and server.

Implementations SHOULD support IPsec with IKE for key management. IPsec ESP with a non-null encryption transform and authentication SHOULD be used. When it is used, 3DES-CBC MUST be supported, AES-CBC SHOULD be supported, HMAC-SHA1-96 MUST be supported, and DES-CBC SHOULD NOT be used.

The memo also warns about privacy: because messages carry the User-Name and NAS address, a snooper may learn the geographic location of peers in real time. It further explains that IKE Main Mode with pre-shared keys SHOULD NOT be used where clients get addresses dynamically; Aggressive Mode SHOULD be used instead. The memo defines no new IANA registries or attributes.
sections.eli5: Anyone listening on the line could learn who is logging in and where. So the guard and the call center talk in a locked code, which is what IPsec provides.
